analysis.one_liner: Expands public reporting of toxic chemical releases and requires disclosure of toxic chemicals in children's products.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 147 cosponsors, including 15 Republicans, but never received a committee vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded the nation's public right-to-know system for toxic chemicals. It would have required companies to report releases of especially dangerous chemicals like lead, mercury, and dioxin down to very low thresholds, publish a government list of carcinogens and other toxins and disclose which ones are in children's toys and products, and reveal not just how much toxic material a factory releases but how much it uses and ships out in products. The bill died quietly: after being referred to the House Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment Subcommittee in May 1999, it was never marked up, never voted on, and expired when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families living near industrial facilities, parents buying toys and children's products, and factory workers. The bill's own findings argue that disclosure works: when companies must publicly report toxic releases and uses, they tend to reduce them, and people can take steps to protect themselves. Workers would gain a new disclosure of how many employees are exposed to each chemical at a reporting facility, and communities would learn where chemicals like mercury and lead travel once they leave a plant — including what is shipped out in consumer products rather than dumped as waste.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the EPA to set reporting thresholds for toxic chemicals that may present significant risks to children's health or the environment — including lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, and chromium — set low enough to capture at least 80% of all releases of each chemical, and makes dioxin and other bioaccumulative chemicals subject to release reporting. [S2] [S3]

It directs the National Toxicology Program to publish an annual list of substances toxic due to carcinogenic, neurotoxic, or reproductive effects, and requires manufacturers and importers of toys and other children's products containing those substances to report the chemicals and their concentrations to the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which must publish the information publicly. [S2] [S3]

It expands toxic release reporting to include occupational exposure data and 'materials accounting' — how much of each chemical a facility brings in, consumes, releases as waste, and ships out in products — so the public can see where toxic chemicals go, not just what leaves the smokestack. [S2] [S3]

It adds citizen enforcement: private individuals could sue violators or the agencies for failing to do their jobs, with the bill placing the burden of proof on a product maker claiming a listed substance is harmless, and penalties funding future enforcement and public-awareness work. [S3]

It consolidates and standardizes environmental reporting, giving small businesses a single reporting form and giving the public one point of contact for EPA information on any regulated company or facility. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and other industrial facilities would bear the cost of much more extensive annual reporting on chemical use, flows, and worker exposure. Toy and children's-product manufacturers and importers would bear the cost of testing and reporting every listed toxic substance in their products, with the risk of citizen suits for noncompliance. Some of those costs could ultimately pass through to consumers, and companies would lose some ability to keep chemical-flow data confidential (though the bill preserves trade-secret withholding for parts of the new materials accounting data).

drawbacks.text: The materials accounting and expanded-use reporting are the heaviest compliance burden: facilities would have to track and verify quantities of chemicals brought in, consumed, shipped out, and wasted each year, a substantial new bookkeeping cost for covered plants. [S3]

After a three-year phase-in, the children's-product reporting definition broadens from toys to all consumer products, which would significantly widen the number of manufacturers required to report listed substances. [S3]

Disclosure alone does not ban or restrict any chemical — a company could legally keep putting listed toxins in products as long as it reports them, leaving the burden on consumers and agencies to act on the information. [S3]

The bill preserves trade-secret withholding for portions of the new materials accounting data, so some of the chemical-flow information the public would gain could still be kept confidential. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on a specific set of manufacturers — chemical companies, industrial facilities, and children's-product makers — for bookkeeping and testing, and disclosure does not by itself remove any chemical from the market. The benefit is broad and durable: communities near industrial plants would learn what chemicals are used, released, and shipped through their neighborhoods; parents would learn which listed carcinogens, neurotoxins, and reproductive toxins are in toys and children's products; and the bill's own findings, based on experience with existing right-to-know rules, note that public disclosure has been shown to prompt companies to reduce risks. On balance this is a low-cost, high-benefit transparency measure whose main casualty would be the chemical industry's informational status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee's Health and Environment Subcommittee in May 1999 and never got a markup or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Henry Waxman introduced the bill on May 3, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce. [S1] [S5]
On May 17, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and no further action was ever taken. [S5]
The bill attracted 147 cosponsors — 131 Democrats, 15 Republicans, and 1 Independent. [S4]
The bill never received a committee markup, a subcommittee vote, or a House floor vote, and expired at the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and children's-product makers, who avoided years of expanded public reporting on toxic chemical use, releases, and product contents — and House leadership was spared a floor fight over a bill with broad bipartisan cosponsorship.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical and toy makers, who kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 147 cosponsors to expand toxic chemical disclosure for children's health.

for.name: 15 of 223 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (including Christopher Shays, Jim Leach, and Porter Goss)
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to cosponsor the bill.

against.name: Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and then to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the Congress without a markup or vote.

against.name: Chemical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Widely opposed expansions of toxic release and chemical-use reporting during this period, the type of disclosure this bill would have mandated.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 15 of the 147 cosponsors were Republicans — but the bill sat in the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee and never reached any vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required much more extensive public reporting: lower thresholds capturing 80% of releases for chemicals like lead, mercury, and dioxin, plus disclosure of how much of each chemical facilities use, consume, and ship out in products. More public information tends to push companies to cut toxic releases and uses, which is precisely the cost the industry would have borne.

industries.industry: Toy and children's-product manufacturers and importers
industries.note: Makers of toys and articles for children containing any listed carcinogen, neurotoxin, or reproductive toxin would have to report the substances and concentrations to the CPSC, which would publish them, with citizen suits available for noncompliance. Parents buying products would gain the information manufacturers would otherwise keep private.

industries.industry: Small businesses with chemical reporting duties
industries.note: Expanded reporting would add facilities beyond current coverage, but the bill also consolidates all annual federal environmental reporting for small businesses into a single form and single point of contact, easing paperwork.
